extracted.intended_audience: authors, translators, and editors of scientific articles to be published in English
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing, writing, translating, and submitting scientific manuscripts in English so they are complete, concise, and clear and comply with editorial and ethical standards. Covers structure (title, abstract, IMRaD sections), language, figures/tables, ethics, and journal submission practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript overarching goals
rubrics_metrics.description: To make international scientific communication more efficient, research articles and other scientific publications should be COMPLETE, CONCISE, and CLEAR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are generalized guidelines; apply common sense. Widespread use should increase efficiency of communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful planning and journal selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully plan and conduct your study; do not draft the whole paper until findings are reasonably firm and complete. Before writing, choose the target journal and match your article to its readership and instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain the journal’s instructions to authors and plan overall length, number of figures, and format accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title
rubrics_metrics.description: Title should be unambiguous, understandable to specialists in other fields, and reflect the content of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific, not general or vague. If relevant, mention study period and location, international scientific name of organism, experimental design (eg case study or randomized controlled trial). If study included human subjects of one sex, state it in the title. Information in the title need not be repeated in the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship and author list
rubrics_metrics.description: List all people who contributed substantially to study planning, data collection or interpretation of results and wrote or critically revised the manuscript, approved the final version and agree to be accountable for all aspects of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow ICMJE 2017 criteria. Authors who meet criteria should participate in drafting and approval. Name order should be determined before submission; post-submission changes require all authors' approval and explanation to the editor. Provide affiliations (during study), present correspondence address, and email addresses for all authors. Encourage ORCiD identifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract content and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract should briefly explain BACKGROUND, OBJECTIVES, METHODS, RESULTS (major data, relationships), and CONCLUSIONS and must reflect the content of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use keywords within the abstract to facilitate searching. Research reports should have informative abstracts including actual results; reviews may be indicative. Do not refer to tables/figures or include references unless absolutely necessary (with full bibliographic detail). Ensure all information in the abstract appears in the main body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keywords
rubrics_metrics.description: Include all relevant scientific terms or additional keywords absent from the title and keep keywords specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add more general terms for interdisciplinary significance. For medical texts, use vocabulary from MeSH Browser. When archiving, embed keywords and metadata in the file.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Define all abbreviations used in the article, except those obvious to non-specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide list if required by editors; define abbreviations at first use in the main body; avoid too many different abbreviations and do not abbreviate terms used rarely. Avoid abbreviations in the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the study was needed and specify research objectives or questions; start from general issues and focus to the research question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate the hypothesis you tested if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods: completeness and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe in detail how the study was carried out: study area, data collection, criteria, origin of material, sample size, number of measurements, age/sex of participants or donors, equipment, data analysis, statistical tests, and software used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all factors that could have affected results. Mention biobank sources with full names and identifiers if available. If citing a method in a non-English or inaccessible publication, explain it in your manuscript. Comply with ethical standards (eg WMA Declaration of Helsinki) regarding patient rights, animal testing, environmental protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results: reporting new results and integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the new results of your study; usually published data should not be included here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention all tables and figures in the text in order. Ensure statistical analysis is appropriate. Disaggregate human/animal data by sex. Do not fabricate, distort, exclude important data, or manipulate images—such actions may be scientific fraud (see COPE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion: scope and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present new results in the Discussion. Answer the research questions, compare main results with published data objectively, discuss limitations, and highlight main findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss implications and generalizability (eg for sex differences). Consider findings contrary to your view and support positions only with methodologically sound evidence. Emphasize major conclusions and practical significance at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgements
rubrics_metrics.description: Mention all people who contributed substantially but are not co-authors and acknowledge all sources of funding; disclose conflicts of interest and permissions for reproduced materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended funding sentence format: “This work was supported by the Medical Research Council [grant number xxxx]” or “This research received no specific grant...” Disclose financial/personal links, ask permission for reproduced materials, and acknowledge language professionals/statisticians while clarifying they are not responsible for the final version. Ensure named people give consent to be acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: References: completeness and appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide sources for all information extracted from other publications and include all data necessary to find them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-English publications, give the original title (transliterated if necessary) followed by its English translation in brackets where possible. Avoid citing inaccessible, coercive, or irrelevant references. Cite primary research where appropriate and do not list unpublished data in references unless source described in main body and permission obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate reporting guidelines (eg EQUATOR Network) to provide minimum necessary information about your study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following reporting guidelines helps ensure necessary information is included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comply with journal instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember to comply with the journal’s instructions to authors in respect of abstract length, style of references, and other format requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan article to fit the journal’s preferred format (length, figure limits, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness: avoid irrelevant and redundant information
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include information not relevant to your research questions; avoid copying from previous publications and submitting the same manuscript simultaneously to multiple journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: preliminary publications (eg conference abstracts) and acceptable secondary publications with editor approvals and citation of primary publication. Avoid repeating information across sections, consider if tables/figures are necessary, ensure captions are informative but not very long, delete obvious statements, define long terms before abbreviation and use consistently, express doubts when necessary but avoid excessive hedging, use numerals for numbers unless exceptions apply (CSE 2014).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity: attribution and plagiarism avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly distinguish your original data and ideas from those of others and your earlier publications; provide citations when relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer summarizing/paraphrasing; use quotation marks when copying text literally. Avoid plagiarism and content recycling; follow COPE and other guidelines on text recycling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scientific terminology and translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proper English scientific terms, preferably from native-English texts; avoid literal translations and false friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a word is used mostly in translations and rarely in English, replace it with a commonly known English term. If a scientific term has no English synonym, define it precisely and suggest an acceptable English translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define uncommon or ambiguous terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Define every uncommon or ambiguous scientific term at first use; list synonyms if helpful but then use one consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal nomenclature established by scientific organizations should be preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision in statements and data reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid unclear statements that require the reader to guess meaning; when reporting percentages, clarify what is regarded as 100%; when writing about correlations, make clear which values are being compared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise reference standards and clearly state comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Units, numbers, dates and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer Système International (SI) units and Celsius degrees; use English decimal point (not comma); use thin spaces for grouping digits when exceeding four digits; denote months as words or first three letters to avoid British/American date ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid capital Roman numerals for centuries. Check journal/editor preference for American vs British spelling/notation and apply consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider international readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember the text will be read mainly by foreigners unfamiliar with country-specific conditions/classifications/concepts; include necessary explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide scientific names and local names (eg 'Kampinos Forest (Puszcza Kampinoska)').

rubrics_metrics.name: Text structure and sentence construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences generally should not be very long; structure should be relatively simple with the subject close to its verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid abstract nouns and overuse of the passive voice. When translating, modify sentence structure if necessary to convey the message clearly. Each paragraph should preferably start with a topic sentence that is developed by subsequent sentences. English allows parallel constructions which can aid understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the text cohesive, logically organized, and easy to follow; link sentences, paragraphs, sections, and the end to the beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic guidelines: 1) Link each sentence to the previous, 2) link each paragraph to the previous, 3) link each section to the previous, 4) link the end to the beginning. Linking techniques: use linking words/phrases (eg however, since then) and repeat key words/phrases rather than synonyms to help readers connect ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures and tables: independence and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Make figures and tables easily understandable without reference to the main body of the article; omit data that are not informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All tables/figures must be mentioned in order in the text and numbered. Do not repeat data in both tables and figures. Apply abbreviations only if necessary; define all abbreviations and symbols in captions or footnotes. Use decimal points and provide axis labels and units. Captions should be informative but not very long. Consider whether a text-table is more effective for small datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text-tables: usage and formatting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Text-tables are simple tables with no graphic elements, embedded within a sentence to present small data sets quickly and comprehensibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules: 1) Larger text-tables are less powerful; 2) the preceding sentence acts as a heading and usually ends with a colon; text-tables should have neither headings nor footnotes; 3) indentation should fit layout; 4) font changes may be used with caution; 5) do not use too many text-tables; also apply normal table formatting rules (2-3 effective digits, order rows by size, correct alignment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language matters: word choice and idioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever scientific terms are not necessary, prefer commonly known words; avoid colloquial, idiomatic expressions and phrasal verbs which are hard for non-native speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overuse of abbreviations and avoid abbreviations in abstracts. Define abbreviations at first use; do not abbreviate rarely-used terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense, person, and referents
rubrics_metrics.description: Use past tense to describe how you performed the study and what you found; use present tense for general statements and interpretations or when writing about article content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing about yourself as 'the author(s)'; use 'we' or 'I' or expressions like 'in this study'. Use 'this study' only for your new results. For cited publications use 'that study' or 'those authors' as appropriate. Use 'which' for non-defining clauses and 'that' for defining clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar, punctuation and readability checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure verbs agree in number with their subjects and pronoun references are clear; note irregular plurals; read the text aloud to check punctuation and intonation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All intonation breaks necessary for proper understanding should be denoted with commas or other punctuation marks (eg difference between 'no more data are needed' and 'no, more data are needed'). Ask a colleague to read the whole text to find ambiguous fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling consistency and national variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Be consistent in spelling; follow either British or American rules for spelling and date notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check journal preference and set that spelling in word/grammar check. Appendix lists common British/American differences (eg -ise vs -ize, colour vs color). For chemistry terms follow IUPAC/RSC recommendations where noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid empty words and ambiguous terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use empty words or phrases that do not add information and force readers to supply meaning, as they destroy credibility in scientific articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of empty words/phrases include 'important', 'treated', 'reacted well', 'quality', 'good/bad', 'proper/properly', 'as soon as possible', etc. Replace weak phrases with precise statements (eg give exact blood pressure values).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct use of scientific terms (ambiguity appendix)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use scientific terms exactly and avoid misuse (eg 'trimester' applied incorrectly across species, 'gender' vs 'sex').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong use of scientific terms can lead to confusion and serious consequences—take special care to choose correct terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity: prefer concise alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace wordy or awkward expressions with simpler choices to improve clarity and brevity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix provides paired examples (eg 'due to the fact that' -> 'because', 'utilize' -> 'use', 'prior to' -> 'before', delete unnecessary fragments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical tips for early-career researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider publishing a review article once you have a clear picture of the field; alternatively, publish meta-analyses or database-based research articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each part of an article should preferably be almost understandable without reading other parts since many readers access individual items (abstracts, figures).
